candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9999 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0063 to +0.0169). The evidence is weak when read on its own, though. Every n-gram has a reported relative frequency of 0.000000, and no function names, call targets, strings, or API references are given for any of them. Nearly all the n-grams are generic compiler-generated mnemonic pairs: prologue/epilogue and stack handling (PUSH SUB, ADD POP), call setup (LEA CALL, XOR CALL, CALL ADD, CALL XOR), and branching (TEST JZ, TEST JS, MOV JZ, CMP JL). These appear in almost any compiled ELF and do not point to mining behavior. A few are somewhat more suggestive: XOR XOR, XOR SHL, XOR MOV, and the conditional-move patterns CMOVZ MOV, XOR CMOVNZ, and CMP CMOVZ. These could fit bit-mixing or branchless arithmetic of the kind found in hashing or proof-of-work loops, but they are also common in ordinary optimized code. No single n-gram has a SHAP contribution above 0.017, so the prediction rests on many small, diffuse contributions rather than on a distinctive signature. The classifier output is a strong prior toward malicious, but the listed evidence cannot confirm cryptojacking specifically, so I classify it as low-confidence and recommend further verification.
